entry.title: RL and SFT both teach a transformer to reason step by step, but not in the same order

link.title: RL and SFT both teach a transformer to reason step by step, but not in the same order

entry.content:
Nov 26, 2026

RL and SFT both teach a transformer to reason step by step, but not in the same order

Zhanxing Zhu · Joint work with Bochen Lyu, Yiyang Jia and Xiaohao Cai

Read the ICML 2026 paper

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) can both teach a model to write out intermediate steps, or a chain of thought[1]. In our ICML 2026 paper, we ask which steps the model learns first. For a one-layer transformer on a family of sparse Boolean problems, we prove that RL with a reward for every step learns the whole chain in one update. When we train the same model with SFT on its own outputs, it learns one step per update, starting with the first.

Colour means the same thing in every figure:

the input, and anything not learned yet the positions that matter, and correct steps wrong steps, and positions to ignore RL and its rewards SFT and its labels

Labels followed by a small dot • and terms with a dotted underline carry a note. Hover over them, or tap.

1. A task that needs intermediate steps

Why does learning parity need a chain of thought?

We study functions of a long bit string that depend on only a few hidden bits. Parity is the hardest of them to learn directly (Fig. 1).

2. What the transformer has to learn

What exactly changes in the model when it learns the task?

The model is a single attention layer that writes the steps one token at a time, reading what is already there. Learning comes down to where each token looks (Fig. 2).

3. Four ways to supervise the chain

Where does each training method get its feedback?

RL and SFT are not two set-ups but four, depending on what is rewarded and on whose earlier steps the model reads during training (Fig. 3).

4. Same chain, different order of learning

Why does RL learn every step at once and SFT one at a time?

Early in training the model’s own steps are wrong. What matters is whether the feedback for a step still makes sense when the step before it is wrong (Fig. 4).

5. The gradient, update by update

What does the training signal look like in each case?

The proofs rest on one quantity: whether the gradient pushes attention up at a token’s two children and down everywhere else. Laid out as a grid, the difference between the two methods can be seen directly (Fig. 5).

6. The experiment shows the same pattern

Does a trained model actually behave this way?

We tested this prediction on parity with 20 input bits, 16 of them relevant, so the chain has four steps (Fig. 6).

7. It is the feedback, not the method

So is the difference really RL versus SFT?

Putting the four settings side by side gives the paper’s main message (Fig. 7).

Our results suggest two questions to ask when comparing RL with SFT[6]. Which steps receive feedback? During training, does the model read its own earlier steps or the correct ones? Both choices affect how the model learns the chain.

References

  1. Wei et al. Chain of thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models. NeurIPS 2022.
  2. Shalev-Shwartz et al. Failures of gradient-based deep learning. 2017.
  3. Wies et al. Sub-task decomposition enables learning in sequence to sequence tasks. 2023.
  4. Kim and Suzuki. Transformers provably solve parity efficiently with chain of thought. ICLR 2025.
  5. Shao et al. DeepSeekMath: Pushing the limits of mathematical reasoning in open language models. 2024.
  6. Chu et al. SFT memorizes, RL generalizes: A comparative study of foundation model post-training. ICML 2025.

Figure 5 illustrates the gradient pattern our theorems predict. Figure 6 shows the experimental heatmaps from Figures 5 and 6 of our paper, Transformers with RL or SFT Provably Learn Sparse Boolean Functions, But Differently.
entry.summary: Seven animated figures show how a one-layer transformer learns sparse Boolean functions with reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.

entry.title: a post with jupyter notebook
entry.content:
To include a jupyter notebook in a post, you can use the following code:

{::nomarkdown} {% assign jupyter_path = "assets/jupyter/blog.ipynb" | relative_url %} {% capture notebook_exists %}{% file_exists
assets/jupyter/blog.ipynb %}{% endcapture %} {% if notebook_exists == "true" %} {% jupyter_notebook jupyter_path %} {% else %}
<p>Sorry, the notebook you are looking for does not exist.</p>
{% endif %} {:/nomarkdown}

Let’s break it down: this is possible thanks to Jekyll Jupyter Notebook plugin that allows you to embed jupyter notebooks in your posts. It basically calls jupyter nbconvert --to html to convert the notebook to an html page and then includes it in the post. Since Kramdown is the default Markdown renderer for Jekyll, we need to surround the call to the plugin with the ::nomarkdown tag so that it stops processing this part with Kramdown and outputs the content as-is.

The plugin takes as input the path to the notebook, but it assumes the file exists. If you want to check if the file exists before calling the plugin, you can use the file_exists filter. This avoids getting a 404 error from the plugin and ending up displaying the main page inside of it instead. If the file does not exist, you can output a message to the user. The code displayed above outputs the following:

Note that the jupyter notebook supports both light and dark themes.

entry.title: a post with custom blockquotes
entry.content:
This post shows how to add custom styles for blockquotes. Based on jekyll-gitbook implementation.

We decided to support the same custom blockquotes as in jekyll-gitbook, which are also found in a lot of other sites’ styles. The styles definitions can be found on the _base.scss file, more specifically:

/* Tips, warnings, and dangers */
.post .post-content blockquote {
  &.block-tip {
    border-color: var(--global-tip-block);
    background-color: var(--global-tip-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-tip-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-tip-block-title);
    }
  }

  &.block-warning {
    border-color: var(--global-warning-block);
    background-color: var(--global-warning-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-warning-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-warning-block-title);
    }
  }

  &.block-danger {
    border-color: var(--global-danger-block);
    background-color: var(--global-danger-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-danger-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-danger-block-title);
    }
  }
}

A regular blockquote can be used as following:

> This is a regular blockquote
> and it can be used as usual

This is a regular blockquote and it can be used as usual

These custom styles can be used by adding the specific class to the blockquote, as follows:

> ##### TIP
>
> A tip can be used when you want to give advice
> related to a certain content.
> {: .block-tip }
TIP

A tip can be used when you want to give advice related to a certain content.

> ##### WARNING
>
> This is a warning, and thus should
> be used when you want to warn the user
> {: .block-warning }
WARNING

This is a warning, and thus should be used when you want to warn the user

> ##### DANGER
>
> This is a danger zone, and thus should
> be used carefully
> {: .block-danger }
DANGER

This is a danger zone, and thus should be used carefully

entry.title: a post with table of contents on a sidebar

link.title: a post with table of contents on a sidebar

entry.content:
This post shows how to add a table of contents as a sidebar.

Adding a Table of Contents

To add a table of contents to a post as a sidebar, simply add

toc:
  sidebar: left

to the front matter of the post. The table of contents will be automatically generated from the headings in the post. If you wish to display the sidebar to the right, simply change left to right.

Example of Sub-Heading 1

Jean shorts raw denim Vice normcore, art party High Life PBR skateboard stumptown vinyl kitsch. Four loko meh 8-bit, tousled banh mi tilde forage Schlitz dreamcatcher twee 3 wolf moon. Chambray asymmetrical paleo salvia, sartorial umami four loko master cleanse drinking vinegar brunch. Pinterest DIY authentic Schlitz, hoodie Intelligentsia butcher trust fund brunch shabby chic Kickstarter forage flexitarian. Direct trade cold-pressed meggings stumptown plaid, pop-up taxidermy. Hoodie XOXO fingerstache scenester Echo Park. Plaid ugh Wes Anderson, freegan pug selvage fanny pack leggings pickled food truck DIY irony Banksy.

Pinterest DIY authentic Schlitz, hoodie Intelligentsia butcher trust fund brunch shabby chic Kickstarter forage flexitarian. Direct trade cold-pressed meggings stumptown plaid, pop-up taxidermy. Hoodie XOXO fingerstache scenester Echo Park. Plaid ugh Wes Anderson, freegan pug selvage fanny pack leggings pickled food truck DIY irony Banksy.

Customizing Your Table of Contents

If you want to learn more about how to customize the table of contents of your sidebar, you can check the bootstrap-toc documentation. Notice that you can even customize the text of the heading that will be displayed on the sidebar.

entry.title: displaying beautiful tables with Bootstrap Tables

link.title: displaying beautiful tables with Bootstrap Tables

entry.content:
Using markdown to display tables is easy. Just use the following syntax:

| Left aligned | Center aligned | Right aligned |
| :----------- | :------------: | ------------: |
| Left 1       |    center 1    |       right 1 |
| Left 2       |    center 2    |       right 2 |
| Left 3       |    center 3    |       right 3 |

That will generate:

Left aligned Center aligned Right aligned
Left 1 center 1 right 1
Left 2 center 2 right 2
Left 3 center 3 right 3

It is also possible to use HTML to display tables. For example, the following HTML code will display a table with Bootstrap Table, loaded from a JSON file:

<table id="table" data-toggle="table" data-url="{{ '/assets/json/table_data.json' | relative_url }}">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th data-field="id">ID</th>
      <th data-field="name">Item Name</th>
      <th data-field="price">Item Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
</table>
ID Item Name Item Price

By using Bootstrap Table it is possible to create pretty complex tables, with pagination, search, and more. For example, the following HTML code will display a table, loaded from a JSON file, with pagination, search, checkboxes, and header/content alignment. For more information, check the documentation.

<table
  data-click-to-select="true"
  data-height="460"
  data-pagination="true"
  data-search="true"
  data-toggle="table"
  data-url="{{ '/assets/json/table_data.json' | relative_url }}"
>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th data-checkbox="true"></th>
      <th data-field="id" data-halign="left" data-align="center" data-sortable="true">ID</th>
      <th data-field="name" data-halign="center" data-align="right" data-sortable="true">Item Name</th>
      <th data-field="price" data-halign="right" data-align="left" data-sortable="true">Item Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
</table>
ID Item Name Item Price
entry.summary: an example of how to use Bootstrap Tables
